1.word_for_word: śrī-gaṇeśāya namaḥ — obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa; viśva-sarga-visargādi-nava-lakṣaṇa-lakṣitam — characterized by the nine topics beginning with primary creation and secondary creation; śrī-kṛṣṇākhyam — known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa; param dhāma — the supreme abode or reality; jagad-dhāma — the abode of the universe; namāma tat — we bow to that; daśame — in the Tenth Canto; daśamam lakṣyam — the tenth topic; āśrita-āśraya-vigraham — embodied as the shelter of those who take shelter; krīḍat yadu-kula-ambhodhau — sporting in the ocean of Yadu’s dynasty; parānandam — supreme bliss; udīryate — is proclaimed; kṛṣṇa-sat-kīrti-vitānāya — for spreading the true and glorious fame of Kṛṣṇa; dharma-glāni-nimittaḥ — occasioned by the decline of dharma; nirodhaḥ duṣṭa-bhūbhujām — the destruction or suppression of wicked rulers; prākṛtādiḥ caturdhā nirodhaḥ — the fourfold dissolution beginning with the prākṛta type; tat-tat-prasaṅgataḥ — as each topic arose; sṛṣṭi-saṃhārādi-nirūpaṇaiḥ — through descriptions of creation, dissolution and the like; kṛtāḥ navatiḥ adhyāyāḥ — ninety chapters have been composed; kṛṣṇa-kīrtaye — for the glorification of Kṛṣṇa; ādau caturbhiḥ adhyāyaiḥ — first, in four chapters; brahma-prārthanayā — following Brahmā’s prayer; avaneḥ bhāram hartum — to remove the burden of the earth; hareḥ janma — Hari’s birth; sa-prasaṅgam — together with its circumstances; nirūpyate — is described; gokule mathurāyām ca dvāravatyām — in Gokula, Mathurā and Dvāravatī; tataḥ kramāt — successively; kṛṣṇa-līlā tridhā proktā — Kṛṣṇa’s līlā is stated in three divisions; tat-tat-bhedaiḥ anekadhā — manifold through the subdivisions of each; sa-pañcatriṃśat-adhyāyaiḥ — in thirty-five chapters; bṛhad-vṛndāvanādiṣu gokule — in Gokula, including Bṛhad-vṛndāvana and the other places; vasataḥ līlā — the līlā of Him dwelling there; sura-duṣkarā — difficult even for the gods; ekena — in one chapter; yamunā-vāriṇi — in the water of the Yamunā; akrūreṇa kṛtā stutiḥ — the praise offered by Akrūra; ekādaśabhiḥ — in eleven chapters; līlā madhuvane kṛtā — the līlā performed in Madhupurī/Mathurā; śeṣaiḥ — in the remaining chapters; dvāravatī-līlā — the Dvāravatī līlā; tat-nirmāṇādi — beginning with its construction; viśadārthakāḥ — having clearly unfolded subject matter; prathame — in the first chapter; kaṃsaḥ — Kaṃsa; sva-mṛtyum devakī-sutāt śrutvā — hearing that his death would come from Devakī’s son; bhītaḥ — frightened; avadhīt tasyāḥ ṣaḍ-garbhān — killed her six sons/embryos; kṛṣṇāvatāra-carita-śravaṇāmṛta-nirvṛtaḥ — delighted by the nectar of hearing the account of Kṛṣṇa’s descent; uktānuvādena — by repeating what has already been said; autsukyāt — out of eagerness; rājā pṛcchati tat punaḥ — the king asks about it again.
1.translation: Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa. I bow to that supreme reality known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the abode of the universe, characterized by the nine topics beginning with creation and secondary creation. In the Tenth Canto the tenth topic, the supreme shelter, is proclaimed in embodied form as the supreme bliss sporting in the ocean of Yadu’s dynasty. For the spreading of Kṛṣṇa’s glorious fame, the destruction of wicked rulers occasioned by the decline of dharma is narrated. The fourfold dissolution beginning with the prākṛta type has already been described as the relevant occasions arose, through accounts of creation, dissolution and the like. Ninety chapters are composed in the Tenth Canto for Kṛṣṇa’s glorification. First, in four chapters, Hari’s birth for removing the burden of the earth, following Brahmā’s prayer, is described together with its circumstances. Kṛṣṇa’s līlā is then presented in three successive divisions—Gokula, Mathurā and Dvāravatī—with many subdivisions within each. In thirty-five chapters the līlā of His residence in Gokula, including Bṛhad-vṛndāvana and other places, a līlā difficult even for the gods, is described. One chapter contains Akrūra’s praise in the waters of the Yamunā, and eleven chapters narrate the līlā performed in Mathurā. The remaining chapters describe the Dvāravatī līlā beginning with the construction of that city. In this way the ninety chapters of the Tenth Canto unfold their subject clearly. In the first chapter it is told that Kaṃsa, frightened after hearing that his death would come from a son of Devakī, killed her six sons. Delighted by the nectar of hearing the account of Kṛṣṇa’s descent, King Parīkṣit eagerly asks about it again by recalling what has already been narrated: ‘The expansion of the dynasties has been described…’

2.word_for_word: aṁśena iti — by the word “aṁśena”; pratītya — according to what is understood or conceived; abhiprāyeṇa — with the intended sense; uktam — it is stated.
2.translation: The word “aṁśena” is used according to the intended or understood sense.

3.word_for_word: nanu — an objection: but; uktāni — these things have already been stated; jātaḥ gataḥ pitṛ-gṛhāt vrajam edhita-arthaḥ ity-ādinā — by statements such as “He was born and went from His father’s house to Vraja, His purpose fulfilled,” and so on; satyam — true; punaḥ — again; vistareṇa — in detail; vada — tell; iti āha — thus he says; avatīrya iti — by the verse beginning “avatīrya.”
3.translation: One may object that these events have already been stated, beginning with the account that He was born and went from His father’s house to Vraja. True; the king now asks, by the verse beginning “avatīrya,” that they be told again in detail.

4.word_for_word: atra loke — in this world; tri-vidhāḥ janāḥ — people are of three kinds; muktāḥ — liberated persons; mumukṣavaḥ — seekers of liberation; viṣayiṇaḥ ca — and those attached to sense objects; teṣām madhye — among them; na kasyāpi alam-pratyayaḥ — no one has the thought “enough” with regard to this narration; nivṛtta-tarṣaiḥ — by those whose thirst has ceased; gata-tṛṣṇaiḥ muktaiḥ — by liberated persons whose craving is gone; mumukṣūṇām ayam eva upāyaḥ — for seekers of liberation this alone is the means; bhava-auṣadhāt — because it is the medicine for worldly existence; viṣayiṇām paramaḥ viṣayaḥ ayam eva — for sense-enjoyers this itself is the highest object of enjoyment; śrotra-mano-’bhirāmāt — because it delights the ear and mind; paśu-ghnaḥ — one who destroys his own self, or an animal-killer.
4.translation: In this world there are three kinds of people: the liberated, those seeking liberation and those attached to sense enjoyment. None of these becomes satiated with this narration. “Those whose thirst has ceased” means liberated persons whose craving is gone. For seekers of liberation, this narration itself is the medicine for worldly existence; for sense-enjoyers, it is itself the supreme object of enjoyment because it delights the ear and mind. The exception is the paśughna, understood as one who destroys his own self, or alternatively as an animal-killer.

5.word_for_word: kiṃ ca — moreover; asmat-kula-daivatam kṛṣṇaḥ — Kṛṣṇa is the deity of our family; ataḥ — therefore; tat-kathā eva nityam śrotavyā — His narration alone should always be heard; pitāmahāḥ iti — this is expressed by the word “grandfathers”; amarān jayanti ye — those who conquer the immortals/gods; devavrataḥ — Devavrata, Bhīṣma; tad-ādyaiḥ atirathaiḥ timiṅgilaiḥ — by mighty chariot-warriors beginning with him, like timiṅgila monsters; duratyayam — very difficult to cross; vatsa-padam iva — like the impression of a calf’s hoof; ati-alpam kṛtvā, tucchīkṛtya — making it extremely small, treating it as insignificant; ataran sma — they crossed; yaḥ śrī-kṛṣṇaḥ eva plavaḥ yeṣām — those whose very boat was Śrī Kṛṣṇa; tasya vīryāṇi vadasva — tell His heroic deeds.
5.translation: Moreover, Kṛṣṇa is the deity of our family; therefore His narrations should always be heard. The word “grandfathers” refers to those who could conquer even the gods. Devavrata, Bhīṣma, and the other great chariot-warriors were like timiṅgila monsters, yet they crossed the otherwise impassable ocean of the Kaurava army after making it as insignificant as a calf’s hoof-print, because Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself was their boat. Thus the request is connected with the earlier verse: tell us of His heroic deeds.

6.word_for_word: na kevalam pāṇḍavān eva arakṣat — He did not protect only the Pāṇḍavas; idam mama śarīram api — this body of mine also; yaḥ rakṣitavān — He protected; drauṇeḥ aśvatthāmnaḥ brahmāstreṇa — by the brahmāstra of Aśvatthāmā, Droṇa’s son; dagdham — scorched; idam mat-śarīram — this body of mine; kurūṇām pāṇḍavānām ca santānasya nidānam — the basis for continuation of both the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas; mama mātuḥ kukṣau praviṣṭaḥ — entering my mother’s womb; dhṛta-cakraḥ — holding the disc; yaḥ jugopa — He protected it.
6.translation: He did not protect only the Pāṇḍavas; He also protected this very body of mine. Scorched by the brahmāstra of Aśvatthāmā, son of Droṇa, my body was the basis for the continuation of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava line. Entering my mother’s womb while bearing His disc, He protected me.

7.word_for_word: akhila-deha-bhājām — of all embodied beings, all living creatures; antaḥ ca bahiḥ ca — both within and without; puruṣa-rūpeṇa — in the form of the indwelling Person; kāla-rūpaiḥ ca — and in forms of Time; aṁśa-abhiprāyeṇa bahu-vacanam — the plural is used with reference to divisions or manifestations; mṛtyum — death, or saṃsāra; amṛtam api — and immortality/liberation; prayacchataḥ — of Him who bestows; vīryāṇi vadasva — tell His heroic deeds; antar-dṛṣṭīnām — for those whose vision is inward; antaryāmi-rūpeṇa — in the form of the Inner Controller; muktim — liberation; bahiḥ-dṛṣṭīnām — for those whose vision is outward; kāla-rūpeṇa — in the form of Time; mṛtyum — death; dadāti — He gives.
7.translation: For all embodied beings He is present within and without, as the indwelling Person and in the forms of Time; the plural is used with reference to the various divisions or manifestations of Time. He bestows both death, that is, saṃsāra, and immortality. The sense is that to those whose vision is turned inward He grants liberation as the Inner Controller, whereas to those whose vision remains outward He gives death in the form of Time. Therefore His heroic deeds alone should be heard with inward vision.

8.word_for_word: nanu — an objection; rohiṇyāḥ tanayaḥ rāmaḥ proktaḥ — Rāma has been stated to be Rohiṇī’s son; vasudevaḥ tu rohiṇyām ... udapādayata — Vasudeva begot sons in Rohiṇī, as the cited genealogy states; vasudevaḥ tu devakyām aṣṭa putrān ajījanat — yet another genealogy says Vasudeva begot eight sons in Devakī; saṅkarṣaṇam ahīśvaram — including Saṅkarṣaṇa, lord of the serpent race; aṣṭamaḥ ... svayam eva hariḥ — and Hari Himself as the eighth; punaḥ devakyā garbha-sambandhaḥ tasya eva uktaḥ — thus a relation of that same Saṅkarṣaṇa to Devakī’s womb is also stated; saḥ kutaḥ ghaṭate — how can that be reconciled?; iti ākṣepaḥ — this is the objection.
8.translation: The objection is this. Rāma, Saṅkarṣaṇa, has been described as Rohiṇī’s son, and the genealogy states that Vasudeva begot sons in Rohiṇī. Yet another genealogy counts Saṅkarṣaṇa among the eight sons connected with Devakī’s womb, with Hari Himself as the eighth. How, then, can the same Saṅkarṣaṇa have a relation to Devakī’s womb? That is the question being raised.

9.word_for_word: kasmāt iti — the force of the word “why”; bhagavataḥ — in the case of Bhagavān; kaṃsa-bhaya-śaṅkāyāḥ — the supposition of fear of Kaṃsa; asambhavāt — because it is impossible; iti arthaḥ — this is the meaning.
9.translation: The force of the question “why?” is that it is impossible to suppose that Bhagavān went to Vraja out of fear of Kaṃsa.

10-12.word_for_word: mātuḥ bhrātaram kaṃsam — Kaṃsa, His mother’s brother; tasmāt vadhān-arham — therefore not fit to be killed; addhā — directly, personally; kasmāt avadhīt — why did He kill him?
10-12.translation: Since Kaṃsa was His mother’s brother and therefore not a proper object of killing, why did Kṛṣṇa personally kill him?

13.word_for_word: nanu — an objection; kṣut-tṛḍbhyām pīḍitasya tava — for you, afflicted by hunger and thirst; kutaḥ śravaṇa-avakāśaḥ — how is there any opportunity for hearing?; tatra āha naiṣā iti — he answers with the verse beginning “naiṣā”; tyakta-udakasya api — even though I have given up water; mama jīvanam — my life; hari-kathā-amṛta-pāna-nimittam — depends upon drinking the nectar of Hari’s narration; tat-uparame — when that ceases; sadyaḥ eva jīvitam na syāt — life would immediately cease.
13.translation: One might ask: since you are afflicted by hunger and thirst, how can you have any opportunity to hear? The king answers with “naiṣā.” Even though I have given up water, my life now depends on drinking the nectar of Hari’s narrations; if that drinking were to stop, my life would immediately cease.

14.word_for_word: evam — thus; sādhu-vādam — a good, proper statement, here a well-formed question; samīcīnam praśnam — an appropriate question; bhāgavata-pradhānaḥ — the foremost among the Bhāgavatas; bhāgavataṣu śreṣṭhaḥ — the best among devotees of Bhagavān.
14.translation: “Sādhu-vāda” means a proper and excellent question. “Bhāgavata-pradhāna” means the foremost, the best among the Bhāgavatas.

15.word_for_word: vyavasitā — firmly resolved, having reached a settled determination; kṛta-niścayā — firmly decided; yat — because, in the sense of “inasmuch as”; yataḥ buddheḥ — because of this settled intelligence.
15.translation: “Vyavasitā” means firmly resolved, with a settled determination. The word “yat” carries the sense of “because”: your intelligence is rightly fixed because unwavering attachment to the narrations of Vāsudeva has arisen in you.

17.word_for_word: tatra tāvat — first, at this point; prathamam bhagavad-avatāra-kāraṇam āha — he states the cause of Bhagavān’s descent; bhūmiḥ ity-ādi-navabhiḥ ślokaiḥ — in the nine verses beginning with “bhūmiḥ”; dṛpta-nṛpa-vyājāḥ ye daityāḥ — demons who had taken the guise of arrogant kings; teṣām anīka-śatānām ayutaiḥ — by tens of thousands of their hundreds of military divisions; yaḥ bhūri-bhāraḥ — the enormous burden; tena ākrāntā — oppressed by that.
17.translation: First, in the nine verses beginning with “bhūmiḥ,” the cause of Bhagavān’s descent is stated. Earth had been oppressed by the enormous burden created by tens of thousands of armies belonging to demons who had assumed the guise of arrogant kings.

18.word_for_word: vibhoḥ antike — in the presence of the mighty lord; upasthitā satī — having approached and stood before him.
18.translation: She came and stood in the presence of the mighty lord, Brahmā.

21.word_for_word: pauruṣīm — belonging to the Puruṣa; puruṣasya bhagavataḥ iyam pauruṣī — this speech belongs to the Supreme Person, Bhagavān; tām gām vācam — that utterance, that speech; me mattaḥ — from me; āśu śṛṇuta — hear quickly; mā ciram — do not delay; avilambatam — let there be no delay; tathā eva vidhīyatām — let it be carried out exactly so.
21.translation: “Pauruṣī” means belonging to the Supreme Person, Bhagavān. Hear from me at once that utterance of His. Do not delay; let exactly what He has ordered be carried out without delay.

22.word_for_word: vijñāpanāt purā eva — even before the petition was made; puṃsā īśvareṇa — by the Supreme Person, the Lord; jvaraḥ — the fever or distress; tāpaḥ — the affliction; avadhṛtaḥ, avadhāritaḥ — had been perceived and ascertained.
22.translation: Even before the petition was made, the Supreme Person, the Lord, had already perceived and ascertained the earth’s distress.

25.word_for_word: devakī-garbha-saṅkarṣaṇa — for the drawing or transfer of the embryo from Devakī’s womb; yaśodāyām — in Yaśodā; sambhaviṣyati — she will appear or be born.
25.translation: She will appear for the transfer of the embryo from Devakī’s womb and will take birth in Yaśodā.

27.word_for_word: bhojendra-bandhanāgāre avatārāya — for the Lord’s descent in the prison of the Bhoja king; prastāva-kathām āha — he begins the introductory narrative; śūrasena ity-ādinā — with the verse beginning “Śūrasena”; yāvat adhyāya-samāpti — continuing to the end of the chapter; mathurām āvasan — dwelling in Mathurā; mathurāyām vasan — living in Mathurā; viṣayān — territories; deśān — regions or lands.
27.translation: To introduce the circumstances leading to the Lord’s descent in the prison of the Bhoja king, the narrative beginning with Śūrasena is now given and continues to the end of the chapter. “He inhabited Mathurā” means that he lived in Mathurā, and “viṣayān” means territories or regions.

29.word_for_word: sūryayā — glossed here as “with the newly wedded woman”; navōḍhayā — with the newly married bride; prayāṇe — at the departure; prayāṇārtham — for the purpose of setting out.
29.translation: The expression describing Devakī here is glossed as “the newly wedded bride,” and “prayāṇe” means “for the purpose of setting out on the journey.”

30.word_for_word: raśmīn — the reins; pragṛhān — the reins or controls held in the hand.
30.translation: “Raśmīn” means the reins, the controls of the horses held in the hand.

31.word_for_word: pāribarham — the accompanying equipment or bridal gifts; upaskaram — equipment, furnishings or paraphernalia.
31.translation: “Pāribarham” means the equipment or paraphernalia supplied with the bride.

34.word_for_word: ābhāṣya — having addressed; re re kaṃsa iti sambodhya — calling out, “Ho, Kaṃsa!”; hantā — a killer; haniṣyati — he will kill.
34.translation: The bodiless voice first addressed him directly, as if saying, “Ho, Kaṃsa!” The word “hantā” means “he will kill you.”

35.word_for_word: kula-pāṃsanaḥ — a disgrace or defilement to the family; kula-dūṣaṇaḥ — one who brings shame upon the dynasty; ārabdhaḥ — set upon, intent on acting; udyuktaḥ — ready or engaged; kace — by the hair; keśa-bandhe — at the knot or bound hair.
35.translation: “Kula-pāṃsana” means one who disgraces his family. “Ārabdha” means that he had set himself to the act, and “kace” means that he seized her by the bound hair.

36.word_for_word: nṛśaṃsam — cruel; krūram — merciless; mahā-bhāga iti — the expression “mahā-bhāga” is significant; sva-janmani harṣeṇa devaiḥ ānaka-dundubhi-ghoṣaṇāt — because at Vasudeva’s own birth the gods joyfully sounded ānaka and dundubhi drums; bhāvi-bhagavad-avatāreṇa — through the future descent of Bhagavān; śakya-pratīkāratā sambhavati — the possibility of a remedy would arise; sāntvayan — while pacifying him; stutyā — through praise; kṛpā-viṣayatvena — by presenting Devakī as an object of compassion; upapattibhiḥ ca — and through reasoned arguments; sāma-mārgeṇa sambodhayan — addressing him by the conciliatory method.
36.translation: “Nṛśaṃsa” means cruel. The description of Vasudeva as “mahā-bhāga” is significant: at his birth the gods had joyfully sounded ānaka and dundubhi drums, indicating that a remedy would become possible through the future descent of Bhagavān. Thus Vasudeva tried to pacify Kaṃsa by the method of conciliation—praising him, presenting Devakī as an object of compassion and giving reasoned arguments.

37.word_for_word: kiṃ ca — moreover; sāma-bhedābhyām sambodhayan — addressing him by conciliation and division; sāma pañca-vidham — conciliation is fivefold; bhedaḥ dvi-vidhaḥ — division is twofold; sambandha — relationship; lābha — benefit; upakṛtiḥ — assistance or advantage; abhedaḥ — identification or non-separation; guṇa-kīrtanam — praise of qualities; dṛṣṭa-adṛṣṭa-bhayam vacaḥ — speech invoking visible and invisible dangers; ślāghanīya-guṇa iti guṇa-kīrtanam — “you possess praiseworthy qualities” is praise; bhaginīm iti sambandha-kathanam — “sister” states the relationship; putrikopamā iti abhedam vakṣyati — “like a little daughter/doll” will express closeness or identification; hanyāt iti strī-vadha-nivṛttyā yaśo-lābham darśayati — by “would he kill?” he points to the fame gained by refraining from killing a woman; udvāha-parvaṇi iti santāna-vṛddhi-upakāram darśayati — “at the wedding” points to the benefit of increasing the family line.
37.translation: Vasudeva now addresses Kaṃsa through the strategies of conciliation and division. Conciliation is said to be fivefold, involving relationship, benefit, assistance, identification and praise of qualities, while division invokes visible or unseen danger. Thus “you possess praiseworthy qualities” praises Kaṃsa’s virtues; “sister” reminds him of their relationship; the later comparison with a little daughter expresses closeness; the question “would you kill her?” points to the fame gained by refraining from killing a woman; and “at the wedding” points to the benefit of allowing the family line to increase.

38.word_for_word: maraṇa-bhayena hanmi iti cet — if one says, “I will kill because I fear death”; maraṇasya apariharaṇīyatvāt — because death cannot be avoided; dehāntarasya avaśyam-bhāvitvāt — because another body must inevitably follow; tatra api bhoga-prema-āspadatvādīnām aviśeṣāt — because the same conditions of enjoyment and attachment apply there as well; tad-bhayena pāpa-ācaraṇam ayuktam — committing sin from that fear is unreasonable; dehena saha — together with the body; vidhātrā lalāṭe likhitatvāt — because it is written on the forehead by the creator, that is, fixed by destiny; adya vā abda-śata-ante vā — today or after a hundred years; avaśyam-bhāvini maraṇe — when death is inevitable; vilamba-mātrāya — merely to delay it; na pāpa-ācaraṇam yuktam — sinful conduct is not justified.
38.translation: If Kaṃsa thinks, “I will kill her because I fear death,” the answer is that death cannot be avoided and another embodiment will inevitably follow; the conditions of attachment and experience continue there as well. Therefore it is unreasonable to commit sin merely from fear of death. “Death is born together with the body” means that its occurrence is already fixed by destiny. Whether death comes today or after a hundred years, sinful action is not justified merely to postpone what is inevitable.

39.word_for_word: asmin dehe gate — when this body is gone; yadi dehāntaram na syāt — if there were no other body; tadā yujyeta pāpena api tat-pālanam — then preserving this body even by sinful means might be reasonable; na tu tat asti — but that is not the case; pañcatvam āpanne — when it reaches dissolution; āpanna-prāye — when it is on the point of perishing; karma-vaśāt — under the control of karma; ayatnataḥ eva — without deliberate effort; prathamam dehāntaram prāpya — first obtaining another body; paścāt pūrvam vapuḥ tyajati — afterward abandoning the former body.
39.translation: If no other body existed after this one perished, preserving the present body even through sin might have some rationale; but that is not the case. “When the body reaches dissolution” means when it is on the verge of perishing. Under the force of karma, without deliberate effort, the embodied being first becomes connected with another body and then abandons the former one.

40.word_for_word: atra dṛṣṭāntaḥ — here is the example; vrajan — while moving; ekena agrataḥ nihitena padā tiṣṭhan — standing supported by one foot placed ahead; bhuvam avaṣṭabhya — bracing against the ground; deham bibhrat — supporting the body; paścāt anyena — afterward with the other foot; pūrva-pradeśāt utthāpya — lifting it from its former place; puraḥ nihitena gacchati — he goes forward by placing it ahead; tadvat — in the same way; tṛṇa-jalaukā — a caterpillar/leech on grass; tṛṇāntaram avaṣṭabhya — grasping another blade of grass; pūrvam tṛṇam tyajati — then lets go of the former blade; karma-pathe vartamānaḥ jīvaḥ api — so also a living being moving along the path of karma.
40.translation: The first example is a person walking: while the body is supported by one foot placed ahead, the other is lifted from its former place and then set forward. The second example makes the sequence still clearer: a grass-caterpillar first takes hold of another blade and only then releases the former one. So it is with a living being proceeding along the path determined by karma.

41.word_for_word: deha-viṣayau eva svīkāra-parityāgau — acceptance and abandonment concern bodies alone; dṛṣṭāntaram āha svapna iti — he gives another example, that of dream; dṛṣṭam — what has been seen, such as the sight of a king; śrutam — what has been heard, such as hearing of Indra; tābhyām āhita-saṃskāreṇa manasā — by a mind impressed with those experiences; tat eva anucintayan — thinking repeatedly of them; īdṛśam jāgrat-dṛṣṭa-śruta-sadṛśam deham — a body resembling what was seen or heard while awake; rājādi-rūpam — in the form of a king and so on; kim api aniruktam paśyati — he sees something indeterminate of that sort; tat eva aham iti prapadyate — he comes to think, “I am that”; jāgrat-dehāt apagata-smṛtiḥ bhavati — memory of the waking body disappears; mano-rathena — by daydreaming or mental projection; jāgrati eva dṛṣṭāntaram — the same point is illustrated even while awake.
41.translation: To show that what is accepted and abandoned is only a body, another example is given: a dream. Impressions formed from things seen, such as a king, and things merely heard of, such as Indra, are contemplated by the mind. In dream one then sees some body resembling those waking impressions, begins to think “I am that,” and loses awareness of the waking body. The example of mental fantasy shows the same process even while awake.

42.word_for_word: nanu — an objection; vicitra-deha-hetūnām karmaṇām kṛtatvāt — since the karmas that cause varied bodies have already been performed; deha-viśeṣa-prāptau kim kāraṇam — what determines the attainment of one particular body?; pañcasu guṇeṣu bhūteṣu — among the five elements; māyā-raciteṣu — fashioned by māyā; nānā-deha-rūpeṇa raciteṣu — arranged in the forms of many different bodies; daivena — by destiny; phala-abhimukhena karmaṇā — by karma that is coming to fruition; coditam manaḥ — the mind impelled; yam yam deham — whichever body; deva-tiryag-ādi-rūpam — a divine, animal or other form; prati dhāvati — toward which it runs; abhiniveśena prāptam — attained through intense identification; tatra tatra dehī jāyate — there the embodied being is born; manaḥ kartṛtvāt — since the mind is the agent; tat eva jāyatām — one might say only the mind should be born; prapadyamānaḥ — identifying with it; tat eva aham iti manyamānaḥ — thinking “that itself is I”; tena saha jāyate — he is born together with it.
42.translation: One may ask: since the karmas producing different bodies have already been performed, what determines which particular body is obtained? At death, among the five elements fashioned by māyā into many bodily forms, the mind—impelled by destiny, that is, by karma ready to bear fruit—rushes toward one particular divine, animal or other body. Through intense identification it immediately takes that form, and the embodied being is born there. If one objects that the mind alone is the agent and therefore only the mind should be born, the answer is “prapadyamānaḥ”: the self identifies with it, thinking “that is I,” and is therefore born together with it.

43.word_for_word: nanu — an objection; bhaviṣyati eva kim api deha-mātram — some future body will indeed arise; tathā api asya ati-priyasya rāja-dehasya rakṣaṇāya akṛtyam api kriyate — nevertheless one might do even what should not be done to protect this very dear royal body; jyotiḥ iti — the answer is the example of light; candra-ādi-jyotiḥ — light such as the moon; udaka-yukteṣu pārthiveṣu ghaṭādiṣu — reflected in earthen pots containing water; udakeṣu pārthiveṣu taila-ghṛtādiṣu ca — or in water and earthly substances such as oil and ghee; samīrasya vegasya anugatam — following the movement of wind; kampādi-yuktam pratīyate — appears to tremble and move; svāvidyā-raciteṣu guṇeṣu deheṣu — in bodies fashioned by one’s own ignorance; rāgeṇa anugataḥ praviṣṭaḥ — entering them under the influence of attachment; muhyati abhiniveśam prāpnoti — he becomes deluded and identifies with them; anyonya-dharma-adhyāsāt — through mutual superimposition of properties; deha-dharmāḥ kārśyādayaḥ ātmani pratīyante — bodily qualities such as thinness appear to belong to the self; ātma-dharmāḥ prema-āspadatvādayaḥ dehādiṣu — properties of the self, such as being an object of love, are attributed to the body; rāja-sūkara-dehayoḥ viśeṣa-abhāvāt — because there is no ultimate difference between a king’s body and a boar’s body; vyarthaḥ mṛtyu-pratīkāraḥ — attempts to ward off death are futile.
43.translation: One may say: although another body will certainly arise, it is still worth doing even what is improper to preserve this especially dear royal body. The answer is the example of reflected light. The moon reflected in water-filled earthen vessels, or in water, oil or ghee, appears to tremble when those reflecting media are disturbed by the wind. In the same way the self, entering bodies fashioned by its own ignorance and following attachment to them, becomes deluded and identifies with their changes. Through mutual superimposition, bodily properties such as thinness are attributed to the self, while properties belonging to the self, such as being an object of love, are attributed to the body. From this standpoint there is no essential distinction between the body of a king and that of a boar, and therefore an immoral attempt to ward off bodily death is futile.

44.word_for_word: evam uktam sāma-upāyam upasaṃharan — concluding the conciliatory method just stated; bhedam āha — he introduces the strategy of division or fear; parataḥ — from another; abhidruhyamāṇāt — from the person who is being attacked; tat-sambandhinaḥ ca — and from that person’s relations; yamāt api — and from Yama as well; iha amutra ca — both here and hereafter; bhayam — fear; iti bhedaḥ darśitaḥ — thus the divisive warning is shown.
44.translation: Having concluded the conciliatory argument, Vasudeva now introduces the strategy of warning through fear. “From another” means that one who attacks another has reason to fear both the injured person and that person’s relatives in this world, and Yama in the next.

45.word_for_word: punaḥ sāma eva āha — he again uses conciliation; putrikopamā — like a little girl or doll; dāru-mayī iva — as though made of wood; acetana-prāyā — nearly powerless or unresisting.
45.translation: He again returns to conciliation. “Putrikopamā” depicts her as helpless and childlike, almost like a little wooden doll that offers no resistance.

46.word_for_word: bodhyamānaḥ — being instructed or reasoned with; upadiśyamānaḥ — being advised; svayam dāruṇaḥ — himself cruel; puruṣādān — man-eaters, demons; anuvrataḥ — following them, conforming to their ways.
46.translation: “Bodhyamāna” means that Kaṃsa was being instructed and reasoned with. He was himself cruel and had adopted the ways of the man-eating demons.

47.word_for_word: ānakadundubhiḥ iti padam — the name “Ānakadundubhi”; mahā-bhāga iti atra ukta-abhiprāyam — carries the intention already indicated by the earlier expression “mahā-bhāga”; prativyoḍhum — to counteract; pratikartum — to oppose or remedy; vañcayitum — to outmaneuver or deceive; idam vakṣyamāṇam apatya-arpaṇam — the plan about to be stated of handing over the offspring; anvapadyata — he adopted; jñātvā — after understanding the situation.
47.translation: The name “Ānakadundubhi” recalls the intention already indicated when Vasudeva was called “mahā-bhāga.” Seeking to counter the danger—indeed, to outmaneuver Kaṃsa—he adopted the plan about to be stated: he would hand over the children.

48.word_for_word: nanu — an objection; khalaḥ ayam — this man is wicked; etat na manyeta — he may not accept this argument; iti āśaṅkya — anticipating this; āha — he says; svayam eva mṛtyuḥ iti — the verse beginning “death itself…”
48.translation: Anticipating the objection that this wicked man might not accept the preceding reasoning, Vasudeva introduces a further argument with the statement beginning, “Death itself…”

49.word_for_word: tasmāt — therefore; upekṣā-doṣa-parihārāya — to avoid the fault of doing nothing; evam kariṣyāmi — I will act in this way; pradāya — by handing over; mṛtyave — to death, that is, to Kaṃsa; nanu idam api na eva nyāyyam — objection: even this is not just; sutāḥ iti — he answers with “if sons…”; asyām yadi me jāyeran — if sons should be born to me from her; yad bhāvi tad bhavatu — let whatever is destined then occur; jīvitam tu tāvat bhavet eva — meanwhile life will at least continue; tad-antarā yadi ayam eva mriyeta — if Kaṃsa himself should die in the meantime; tadā na kiñcit anyāyyam — then no injustice will have been done.
49.translation: Therefore, to avoid the fault of simply allowing Devakī to be killed, Vasudeva resolves to act in this way: he will hand over the sons to “death,” meaning Kaṃsa. If one objects that even this is unjust, he reasons: if sons are actually born to me from her, let what is destined happen then; at least life will continue until that time. And if Kaṃsa himself dies in the interval, no such injustice will need to occur.

50.word_for_word: yadi ca sutāḥ bhaviṣyanti na ca ayam mriyeta — if sons are born and Kaṃsa does not die; mat-putrāt eva asya maraṇam iti viparyayaḥ vā kim na syāt — why could there not be a reversal, namely that his death will indeed come from my son?; prauḍhasya kaṃsasya tava bālakāt katham mṛtyuḥ syāt — objection: how could mature Kaṃsa die from a child?; gatiḥ dhātuḥ duratyayā — the course ordained by the Creator is impossible to overcome; dhātuḥ — of the one who declared, “her eighth pregnancy will kill you”; apatyārpaṇa-pratijñā eva mantraḥ — for the present, the pledge to hand over the offspring is the only policy; upasthitaḥ mṛtyuḥ nivarteta — the immediate death may be turned away; nivṛttaḥ punaḥ kālāntare āpatet cet — if, after being averted, it returns later; tadā na aparādhaḥ mama — then the fault is not mine.
50.translation: If sons are born and Kaṃsa does not die beforehand, why could destiny not bring about the very reversal foretold—that his death comes from Vasudeva’s son? If one asks how a grown Kaṃsa could die at the hands of a child, the answer is that the course ordained by the Creator who announced “her eighth pregnancy will kill you” cannot be overcome. For the present, therefore, the pledge to hand over the children is the practical means: it may avert the death that is immediately present. If death returns later in another form, the fault will not lie with Vasudeva.

51.word_for_word: prāṇinām adṛṣṭam — the unseen destiny of living beings; durvitarkyam — impossible to infer with certainty; sa-dṛṣṭāntam āha — he explains with an example; vane vṛkṣān pradahan agniḥ — a fire burning trees in a forest; sannihitān api vṛkṣān parityajya — sometimes passes over trees that are nearby; dūrasthān api dahati — and burns even distant ones; grāme gṛhān vā — likewise houses in a village; prāṇi-adṛṣṭa-vyatirekeṇa kiñcit niyāmakam na asti — there is no visible regulator apart from the unseen destiny of beings; evaṃ jantoḥ janma-maraṇayoḥ hetuḥ — likewise the cause governing a creature’s birth and death; durvibhāvyaḥ acintyaḥ — difficult to discern, inconceivable.
51.translation: The unseen destiny of living beings cannot be reasoned out with certainty, so an example is given. A forest fire may pass over trees standing nearby and burn others farther away; the same may happen among houses in a village. No visible rule apart from the unseen destiny of the beings involved explains this. In the same way, the causes governing a creature’s birth and death are exceedingly difficult to discern.

52.word_for_word: yāvat ātma-nidarśanam — as far as his own insight extended; sva-prajñā-avadhi — up to the limit of his own understanding; vicārya — having reflected.
52.translation: Vasudeva reflected on the matter as far as his own insight and understanding could reach.

53.word_for_word: tasya viśvāsāya — in order to gain his confidence; vikasita-mukha-ambhojaḥ — with his lotus-like face opened and bright; prahasan — smiling; abravīt — he spoke.
53.translation: In order to gain Kaṃsa’s confidence, Vasudeva let his lotus-like face brighten and spoke with a smile.

54.word_for_word: yat yathā aśarīriṇī vāk āha — what the bodiless voice said, exactly as it said it; tathā hi niścitam — is certainly fixed; asyāḥ sakāśāt te bhayam na asti — your danger does not come from Devakī herself; yebhyaḥ putrebhyaḥ te bhayam utthitam — your danger arises from her sons; aṣṭamaḥ hantā iti ukteḥ — because it was said, “the eighth will kill you”; anyonya-apekṣayā — depending on the relative order of counting; sarve api aṣṭamāḥ bhaveyuḥ — any of them might be reckoned as the eighth; sarvān api tān asyāḥ putrān samarpayiṣye — therefore I will hand over all her sons.
54.translation: What the bodiless voice announced is certainly fixed, but it did not say that Devakī herself was the source of danger; the danger was to arise from her sons. Since the prophecy said “the eighth will kill you,” and the position “eighth” can depend on the direction or relative order of counting, Vasudeva promises to hand over all of her sons.

55.word_for_word: tad-vākye sāraḥ — the substance or force in Vasudeva’s words; upapattiḥ — cogent reasoning; tad-vit — understanding that reasoning; nivavṛte — he desisted; nivṛttaḥ — he turned back from the act.
55.translation: The “substance” in Vasudeva’s words was their cogent reasoning. Recognizing that force, Kaṃsa desisted from killing Devakī.

56.word_for_word: prasūti-kāle upāvṛtte prāpte — when the time of delivery arrived; sarvaḥ sarvātmā bhagavān eva devatā yasyāḥ — she whose very deity is Bhagavān, the Self of all; sā tathā — such is the meaning of “sarva-devatā”; sarva-devatā-mayī iti vā — or, one who embodies all the deities; bhagavad-āśrayatvāt — because she is the receptacle or shelter of Bhagavān.
56.translation: “When the time came” means when the time of delivery arrived. Devakī is called “sarva-devatā” because Bhagavān, the Self of all, is her very deity; alternatively, she may be called one who embodies all the deities because she is the chosen receptacle of Bhagavān.

58.word_for_word: mṛtyave putram katham arpitavān — how could he hand his son over to death?; sādhūnām — of truthful and righteous people; satya-sandhānām — of those firmly committed to truth; viduṣām — of those who know; bhagavān eva tattvam na anyat — that Bhagavān alone is the ultimate reality and nothing else; kim akāryam kadaryāṇām — what improper act is impossible for the miserly or base?; dhṛta-ātmānām — of those who hold the Self/Lord firmly in the heart; citte dhṛtaḥ ātmā hariḥ yaiḥ — those by whom Hari is held within the mind; kim dustyajam — what is difficult for them to give up?
58.translation: The verse answers a series of objections. How could Vasudeva hand his son over to death? For truthful, saintly persons, what hardship is unbearable when truth must be kept? How could he give up the happiness of raising his child? For those who know that Bhagavān alone is the ultimate reality, what worldly object must be clung to? Could he have relied on Kaṃsa’s mercy and assumed the child would not be killed? No—there is no deed too improper for the base. And how could Devakī surrender her child? For those who hold Hari firmly in the heart, what is ultimately impossible to relinquish?

62.word_for_word: kaṃsasya śāntiḥ — Kaṃsa’s present state of calm; deva-kārya-anuguṇā na bhavati — would not accord with the work the gods needed accomplished; nāradasya pratyavasthānam — Nārada therefore intervenes or takes a contrary stand; tat āha — this is what the text now states; nandādyā ity-ādi-trayeṇa — in the three verses beginning “Nanda and the others.”
62.translation: Kaṃsa’s present calm would not serve the divine purpose that had to be accomplished. Nārada therefore intervened and reversed that situation, as is described in the three verses beginning with “Nanda and the others.”

63.word_for_word: ubhayor — of both; vasudeva-nanda-kulayoḥ — the families of Vasudeva and Nanda.
63.translation: “Of both” refers to the two families, that of Vasudeva and that of Nanda.

64.word_for_word: vadhodyamam — the undertaking or effort to kill; deva-kṛtam — carried out by the gods; iti śeṣaḥ — these words are to be supplied to complete the sense.
64.translation: The phrase is to be understood as “the effort, undertaken by the gods, to kill the demons.”

66.word_for_word: nigaḍaiḥ — with fetters; śṛṅkhalaiḥ — with chains; ajaḥ — the unborn one; viṣṇuḥ — Viṣṇu; tat-śaṅkayā — because of suspicion or fear that He would appear.
66.translation: “Nigaḍaiḥ” means “with chains.” “Aja,” the Unborn, refers to Viṣṇu; Kaṃsa killed each child because he feared that Viṣṇu might be the one appearing among them.
